To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

e-government does not improve citizens’ trust in the federal agencies that provide services online, but does increase citizens’ confidence in those agencies’ future service delivery performance, and does not affect citizens’ trust in government overall.

(1) E-government does not improve citizen perceptions of the quality of service delivery nor does it improve citizen perceptions of trustworthiness; (2) e-government is associated with greater confidence in the future service delivery of the agency experienced; and (3) the relationship between e- government and trust in government overall is mediated by the relationship between e-gov- ernment and confidence.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relationship between e-govemment and citizen trust is more complicated than many had hoped, but that e-government may still play an important role in helping to restore trust in government.
e-government may not be the panacea for trust problems in government, but it may help improve citizens' perceptions of the agencies they deal with.
e-government is not yet a panacea for the trust deficit that has developed between citizens and government over the past several decades.
The main takeaway from our work is that
e-government is not yet the silver bullet many had hoped.
, although e-government is a potentially powerful tool for improving citizens’ perceptions of the performance of government agencies, it is not yet an effective means of building trust in government.
e-government has not yet been shown to be a transformational medium in terms of improving citizen satisfaction or trust in government, but it may have the potential to do so in the future.
